contrastMetadata.transferBoundary: Classify the strategy from its invariant, legal elimination, data access, and workload—not from words such as sorted, threshold, search, left, right, or mid.

items.prompt: A function contains variables named left, right, and mid, but right decreases by one on every iteration. Which classification is justified?

options.text: It has linear worst-case progress unless another branch provides stronger shrinkage.
It is binary search and therefore O(log n).
It is O(1) because only three variables are used.
It is automatically O(n²) because it has two boundaries.

feedback.reason: Classification follows executed updates and invariant, not identifier names.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Starting with n candidates and decreasing right by one leaves `n-k` candidates after k iterations. Reaching zero can therefore require n iterations; computing or naming mid does not change that recurrence.
Contrast the strategies

O(log n) requires proportional shrinkage, such as retaining at most half after each O(1) step. Three variables describe O(1) auxiliary space, not O(1) time, and two boundaries do not imply nested O(n²) work. Unless another branch removes a constant fraction on every worst-case path, the one-at-a-time path is O(n).

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Measure candidate-set shrinkage along the worst-case execution path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_by_names: Variable names do not determine how fast the candidate set shrinks.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: A constant number of variables bounds auxiliary space, not how many iterations execute.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.quadratic: Two stored boundaries do not create nested iterations or n work per iteration.

items.prompt: A problem statement uses the phrase “find a threshold.” What must be proven before choosing binary search?

options.text: The threshold predicate has one directional transition over an ordered candidate domain.
Nothing else; the word threshold is sufficient.
Only that the input contains numbers.
Only that a midpoint can be computed.

feedback.reason: A threshold label must correspond to an actual boundary in predicate truth.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Define an ordered bounded candidate domain and a predicate P. A false-to-true threshold needs `a <= b` and `P(a) = true` to imply `P(b) = true`; the reverse orientation needs the corresponding true-prefix implication.
Contrast the strategies

That implication turns a midpoint result into proof that one whole side is impossible. The word “threshold,” numeric values, and the ability to compute a midpoint do not prevent a predicate from changing truth more than once, so none is sufficient by itself.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Translate a threshold noun into a quantified one-transition predicate.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.word_threshold: Natural-language wording does not prove that predicate truth changes direction at most once.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.numeric_input: Numeric candidates can still be tested by alternating or otherwise nonmonotonic conditions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.midpoint: Every finite range has a midpoint, including invalid search models.

items.prompt: The input is described as sorted, but the query asks for the first value whose hash has an even final bit. Which strategy follows from the description alone?

options.text: No binary-search conclusion follows; the hash condition may require scanning unless separately indexed.
Binary search is mandatory because sorted appears in the prompt.
Use lower bound on the hash parity.
Check only the middle hash because mid implies logarithmic search.

feedback.reason: The sort key and query property must align.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Sorting constrains the original values, but a hash deliberately remaps them. Even final-bit parity can alternate as values increase, so a true or false midpoint hash does not classify hashes on either side.
Contrast the strategies

Scan in increasing index order to satisfy “first,” unless a separate index of matching positions exists. Binary search from the word sorted, lower bound on hash parity, and checking only mid all assume an order relation between value and hash parity that the prompt does not supply.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A transformed property inherits no order unless that relationship is proved.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_sorted: The condition need not be monotonic in value order.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.lower_bound_hash: Hash parity can alternate and therefore does not form a single lower-bound suffix.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_hash: One midpoint hash result supplies no implication about any unchecked hash on either side.

items.prompt: A loop is named binarySearch but sequentially checks array[i] for i = 0, 1, 2, .... What is it?

options.text: A linear scan.
Binary search because the function name says so.
A logarithmic hybrid because the name and loop differ.
Impossible to classify even with the loop described.

feedback.reason: Algorithm names are claims that must match the implementation.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The executed state visits indices `0,1,2,...` one at a time. In the worst case it inspects n positions, so its mechanism and time are those of a linear scan.
Contrast the strategies

A binary-search name is an undocumented claim, not an operation. No logarithmic hybrid appears when a label and implementation disagree, and the explicit traversal is enough to classify the code. Rename the function to reflect its real behavior or replace the implementation with a proven boundary search if the contract allows it.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Read the state transition before trusting the function name.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_search: Behavior, not the function name, defines the algorithm.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.hybrid_log: The executed work still inspects candidates sequentially; a contradictory name contributes no logarithmic operation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unknown: The prompt explicitly states the traversal order and therefore provides enough behavior to classify it.

items.prompt: A loop uses a variable named scanIndex but halves a proven monotonic candidate interval every iteration. Which classification is correct?

options.text: It implements binary-search structure despite the variable name.
It is a linear scan because the variable is called scanIndex.
It is O(1) because there is one index variable.
It is not a search because mid is not named explicitly.

feedback.reason: The invariant and update rule define the algorithm.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The maintained invariant says the answer remains in an ordered candidate interval. Each predicate result proves one side impossible, and each update retains at most half, giving O(log n) iterations when per-step work is O(1).
Contrast the strategies

Those semantics define binary search even if the inspected midpoint is stored in `scanIndex`. One variable does not make the loop constant-time, and the exact identifier `mid` is not required to compute or use a midpoint.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Classify from candidate meaning, discard proof, and proportional progress.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_by_name: The identifier does not override the proven half-discard update executed by the loop.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: One stored index can be updated O(log n) times before the interval becomes empty.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.not_search: A midpoint can be computed under another identifier.

items.prompt: A solution contains a while loop and two pointers. Is that enough to distinguish binary search from a two-pointer scan?

options.text: No. The candidate invariant and pointer updates must be examined.
Yes. Two pointers always mean binary search.
Yes. A while loop always means a scan.
Yes, if the variables are named left and right.

feedback.reason: Shared syntax is not a strategy boundary.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Both patterns can use `while (left < right)`. Binary search inspects a representative midpoint and rejects a proven region, normally shrinking proportionally. A two-pointer scan inspects endpoint relations and often moves one or both pointers by one.
Contrast the strategies

The same syntax therefore supports different invariants and iteration counts. Two indices, a while loop, or the names left/right cannot distinguish them without the update rule and proof of what each movement eliminates.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Compare what each pointer denotes and how much state each update resolves.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_two_binary: Two-pointer scans also maintain two indices while moving them under a different invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_while_scan: Iterative binary search commonly uses a while loop, so the control construct is shared.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.yes_names: The names left and right appear in both binary searches and endpoint-based scans.

items.prompt: A problem asks for an exact target-value lookup in O(log n), but the input is an unsorted array and no preprocessing or auxiliary index is permitted. What should the analyst do?

options.text: Challenge the stated target or identify missing structure; do not invent an unsound binary search.
Use midpoint discard because the complexity target demands it.
Assume the input is sorted even though it is not stated.
Rename the array to sortedValues.

feedback.reason: Complexity requirements must be reconciled with available structure.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

With only unsorted values, a midpoint mismatch leaves every other position possible. In the comparison model, an adversary can place the target at the last unchecked position, so a correct worst-case lookup must inspect O(n) values.
Contrast the strategies

Report the contradiction and ask for a sorted/indexed precondition, allowed preprocessing, or a revised bound. Forcing midpoint discard can return not found while the target remains unchecked; assuming sorted data changes the input contract; renaming the array changes no bytes or order.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: When the requested bound lacks a supporting invariant, expose the missing contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.force_binary: A desired bound cannot create the value-order implication needed to discard an unsorted half.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.assume_sorted: Treating allowed unsorted inputs as sorted changes the contract and yields wrong results.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.rename_array: Changing an identifier does not reorder the stored values or create an index.

items.prompt: A code review comment says, “This has nested if statements, so it cannot be binary search.” Which response is correct?

options.text: Nested conditionals do not decide the pattern; interval elimination and progress do.
Any nested conditional forces linear scanning.
Binary search must contain exactly one if statement.
Big-O can be read directly from indentation depth.

feedback.reason: Surface control-flow shape is weaker evidence than the maintained invariant.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

A binary search may branch for equality, less/greater comparison, rotated-array half detection, or boundary-specific retention. Those nested conditionals can still leave exactly one proven subinterval.
Contrast the strategies

Complexity follows executed branch paths, recursive calls, and candidate shrinkage—not indentation depth or a required count of if statements. Inspect whether every nonterminal path preserves the invariant and reduces the interval proportionally.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Branches express cases; the state transition determines the algorithm.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.if_forces_scan: Nested branches can still retain only one half and leave logarithmically many iterations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_one_if: Correct implementations can organize equality, direction, and edge cases across several branches.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.complexity_syntax: Runtime follows executed iterations and per-iteration work, not source indentation depth.

items.prompt: The requirement says “closest value.” Does that phrase identify binary search by itself?

options.text: No. It depends on sorted order, access model, tie-breaking, and the exact closeness contract.
Yes. Closest always means binary search.
Yes, and it always means linear scan.
Return the first midpoint because it is geometrically central.

feedback.reason: Problem keywords name an output goal, not necessarily the mechanism.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For a sorted random-access numeric array, a lower bound locates the insertion boundary; only its immediate neighbors can be closest by absolute difference, after which the declared tie rule selects one. That is a proof, not a consequence of the word “closest.”
Contrast the strategies

On unsorted data, with a custom distance metric, missing midpoint access, or a first-original-match tie rule, scanning or another index may be correct. Returning the first midpoint confuses central index position with minimum value distance.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Derive candidate elimination and tie behavior from the exact closeness metric.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_binary: Unsorted data or custom metrics may require other methods.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_scan: Sorted numeric data can support a boundary-based closest lookup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mid_closest: A central index can hold a value far from the target; index centrality does not minimize value distance.

items.prompt: A function computes mid = (left + right) // 2, does O(1) local work, and recursively explores both halves until subarrays contain one element. Which worst-case time is accurate?

options.text: O(n): computing mid does not make the traversal logarithmic when both halves are explored.
Any midpoint recursion is O(log n).
The midpoint calculation is O(1), so the whole function is O(1).
It becomes a scan only if an index is named i.

feedback.reason: The recurrence follows how many subproblems are explored.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The recurrence is `T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(1)`. The recursion tree has n leaves and fewer than n internal nodes, so it performs O(n) total calls and O(n) local work.
Contrast the strategies

Binary search uses `T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1)` because it proves one half irrelevant, giving O(log n). O(1) counts only one call’s midpoint work, and a variable named i has no role in the recurrence. Exploring both disjoint halves visits the whole domain.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Count retained recursive branches at every level, not just recursion depth.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.always_log: Logarithmic search follows one retained half per level; two recursive calls create n leaves.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.constant: The midpoint calculation is constant-time per call, but the recursion executes O(n) calls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.linear_scan_name: Identifiers do not determine how many recursive subproblems the implementation executes.

items.prompt: A sorted array query uses a helper named isValid(mid), but isValid alternates across indices. Which classification is correct?

options.text: It is an arbitrary-condition scan problem unless another structure is added.
It is monotonic because the helper is called isValid.
Passing mid makes it binary-searchable.
Sorted input alone makes the helper monotonic.

feedback.reason: Semantic behavior must be inspected directly.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

For a truth sequence such as false, true, false, true, a midpoint result says nothing about whether earlier or later indices satisfy the helper. The name `isValid` and parameter `mid` describe an interface, not a cross-index implication.
Contrast the strategies

Scan every necessary index unless a new index or monotonic reformulation is provided. Sorted values help only predicates aligned with value order; the prompt explicitly states that this helper alternates, so sortedness cannot make it monotonic.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Treat helper names as documentation claims and verify their truth pattern.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.monotonic_by_name: The truth sequence, not the name, determines monotonicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.binary_by_parameter: Any index can be passed to an arbitrary predicate.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_enough: The helper explicitly alternates, so it does not follow the array’s sorted value relation.

items.prompt: Which observations are insufficient by themselves to classify code as binary search? Select all that apply.

options.text: Variables named left, right, and mid.
The prompt contains the word sorted.
The implementation uses a while loop.
Each midpoint outcome proves one whole side impossible and the interval shrinks proportionally.

feedback.reason: Syntax and vocabulary are weak signals.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Left/right/mid names can wrap a one-step scan, the word sorted may describe an order unrelated to the query, and a while loop is shared by many patterns. None states what a midpoint proves or how much state disappears.
Contrast the strategies

The unselected half-discard statement is substantive: every midpoint outcome proves one side answer-free and proportional shrinkage bounds the number of iterations. That evidence, together with coherent boundaries, supports binary-search classification.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Replace surface resemblance with a proof about remaining candidates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.half_discard_proof: This statement supplies the semantic elimination and proportional progress that define binary-search behavior.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.left_right_mid: The updates may still be linear or incorrect.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sorted_word: The query may not align with the order.

items.prompt: Which evidence should replace keyword-based strategy classification? Select all that apply.

options.text: A statement describing where the answer can still remain.
A proof connecting midpoint outcomes to impossible regions.
A demonstration that every nonterminal step shrinks the candidate set.
Identifiers copied from a standard template.

feedback.reason: Classification should rest on semantic and operational evidence.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

The candidate invariant defines where an answer may remain. The discard implication explains why a midpoint outcome makes a region impossible. The progress measure proves termination and distinguishes one-at-a-time O(n) shrinkage from proportional O(log n) shrinkage.
Contrast the strategies

All three selected observations describe semantics or executed state transitions and can be checked against code. Identifiers copied from a template may improve readability after the proof is established, but copied names can equally label a scan, a nonterminating loop, or an unsound discard.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: A useful classification predicts correctness, progress, and cost from observable behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.familiar_names: Template identifiers can be copied onto code with different updates, invalid elimination, or no progress.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.candidate_invariant: This defines the active search state.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.progress_measure: This determines termination and iteration count.

items.prompt: Which code behaviors are compatible with a linear scan despite binary-search-like names? Select all that apply.

options.text: A boundary moves by exactly one position on every iteration.
Every element is eventually inspected in the worst case.
Midpoint outcomes do not imply anything about unchecked regions.
Exactly one proven half is retained after every mismatch.

feedback.reason: The executed candidate progression defines the method.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

Moving a boundary by one leaves n-1, n-2, and so on candidates. Inspecting every item is the corresponding worst-case work. If midpoint results classify no unchecked region, the midpoint is merely another visited position.
Contrast the strategies

All three selected behaviors are compatible with a linear scan even if the variables look binary-search-like. Retaining exactly one proven half is the control behavior: it supplies proportional elimination and is not scan-like.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Trace the number of unresolved candidates after each worst-case update.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.half_each_time: Retaining one proven half after each mismatch is the proportional elimination characteristic of binary search.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.one_step_boundary: The candidate count may decline linearly.

items.prompt: Which prompt words require further analysis rather than an automatic binary-search choice? Select all that apply.

options.text: sorted.
threshold.
minimum.
A proven false-to-true predicate over a bounded ordered domain.

feedback.reason: Common interview vocabulary identifies hypotheses to test, not guaranteed strategies.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct

“Sorted” leaves open whether the query follows the sort key. “Threshold” leaves open whether truth changes only once. “Minimum” states an optimization goal but not whether feasibility is monotonic. Each is a hypothesis to test.
Contrast the strategies

The unselected statement is different: it declares a bounded ordered domain and a proven false-prefix/true-suffix predicate, which is the mechanism needed for first-true boundary search. It is evidence rather than a lone keyword.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Expand every keyword into the invariant it would need to imply.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.first_true_proof: This phrase already includes the decisive structure rather than a surface keyword.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sorted: The query still must align with the order.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.threshold: The threshold may not represent a monotonic predicate.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.minimum: Optimization alone does not create monotonic feasibility.

items.prompt: A loop uses variables left, right, and mid but removes exactly one candidate per O(1) iteration. Another loop uses variable i and doubles i each O(1) iteration until i >= n. Select the worst-case time of each.
constraints: The first loop starts with n candidates.
The second loop starts at i = 1.

feedback.reason: Variable names can point in the opposite direction from the true complexity.

blocks.text: Why this choice is correct
The first loop removes one of n candidates per O(1) step, so after k steps n-k remain and the worst case needs n steps: O(n). Its left/right/mid names do not change that count.
Contrast the strategies
The second loop visits `1,2,4,...,2^k`. It stops when `2^k >= n`, so `k = ceil(log2 n)` O(1) iterations: O(log n). O(1) ignores repeated updates, while O(n log n) invents n work per iteration.

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.text: Solve the update equation for the first state that meets the termination condition.

contrastSets.transferBoundary: Classify the strategy from its invariant, legal elimination, data access, and workload—not from words such as sorted, threshold, search, left, right, or mid.
